| `tau_jj_s` | s | `1.4` | | code: SUMO documentation, Simulation/Meso: --meso-edgelength 98, --meso-tauff 1.13, --meso-taufj 1.13, --meso-taujf 1.73, --meso-taujj 1.4, --meso-jam-threshold -1, --meso-junction-control |
| `jam_threshold` | - | `null` | | code: SUMO documentation, Simulation/Meso: --meso-edgelength 98, --meso-tauff 1.13, --meso-taufj 1.13, --meso-taujf 1.73, --meso-taujj 1.4, --meso-jam-threshold -1, --meso-junction-control |
| `junction_control` | - | `true` | | code: SUMO documentation, Simulation/Meso: --meso-edgelength 98, --meso-tauff 1.13, --meso-taufj 1.13, --meso-taujf 1.73, --meso-taujj 1.4, --meso-jam-threshold -1, --meso-junction-control |

**Equations.**

- *exit time*: `t_exit = max(t_entry + ℓ / min(v_desired, v_max·f_speed), t_last + τ_xy / lanes, t_green, t_room)` x, y ∈ {free, jammed} for this segment and the next
- *jam*: `jammed ⇔ occupancy > capacity · L / (v_max·τ_ff + L), L = 7.5 m` SUMO's --meso-jam-threshold -1

**Assumptions.**

- One FIFO queue per segment shared by its lanes (Eissfeldt's original), not SUMO's later per-lane queues; the headway is divided by the lane count.
- A blocked departure (red, full segment, refusing boundary) is retried at the next mobility step; a free one keeps its exact instant.
- Positions are the queue's placement, not a trajectory: free-flow motion to the earliest exit, then standing in the queue at the segment's end.

**Limitations.**

- No lane changes, overtaking within a segment, or acceleration: speed is free-flow or zero.
- Unsignalised junctions are only their headways: no priority between approaches.

**Ignores.**

- Speed caps, stops, reroutes and closures sent as commands.
- Weather.

**Sources.**

- paper: Eissfeldt, N. G. (2003). Vehicle-based modelling of traffic: theory and application to environmental impact modelling. PhD thesis, Universität zu Köln.. the queue model: segment capacity, free-flow exit time, jam-dependent headways
- paper: Krajzewicz, D., Erdmann, J., Behrisch, M., Bieker, L. (2012). Recent Development and Applications of SUMO. Int. J. Advances in Systems and Measurements 5(3&amp;4), 128-138.. MESO, SUMO's mesoscopic mode
- code: SUMO documentation, Simulation/Meso: --meso-edgelength 98, --meso-tauff 1.13, --meso-taufj 1.13, --meso-taujf 1.73, --meso-taujj 1.4, --meso-jam-threshold -1, --meso-junction-control

### `mobility/native/medium`

The native mobility engine: it freezes every actor's state at the start of each step, asks the car-following, lane-change and intersection models for one decision per actor from that frozen state, integrates them all together, and publishes `Kinematics` for every actor with the spawn, despawn and signal-state lists. The freeze is what makes the update a Jacobi update and therefore independent of the order the actors are visited in (the determinism contract's Jacobi update).

version `1.0.0`; tiers `abstract`, `medium`; hosting `in-process`; draws random numbers.

| Parameter | Unit | Default | Range | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `step` | s | `0.1` | | standard: assumption (this engine's own definition): mobility step default 100 ms, range 10-100 ms |
| `car_following` | - | `mobility/car-following/idm` | | code: assumption (this engine's native mobility tiers, no external source): the `Mobility` trait and its invariants I-M1, I-M2, I-M4 |
| `intersections` | - | `SignalsAndGapAcceptance` | | code: assumption (this engine's native mobility tiers, no external source): the `Mobility` trait and its invariants I-M1, I-M2, I-M4 |
| `lane_changes` | - | `true` | | code: assumption (this engine's native mobility tiers, no external source): the `Mobility` trait and its invariants I-M1, I-M2, I-M4 |
| `lookahead` | m | `70.0` | | code: legacy/scms_sim_ref/mock_pipeline/run.py: `idm_lookahead_m` 70 m |
| `classes` | - | `["car", "truck", "bus", "moto", "emergency"]` | | code: assumption (this engine's native mobility tiers, no external source): the `Mobility` trait and its invariants I-M1, I-M2, I-M4 |
| `insertion_gap` | m | `2.0` | | code: this crate: a trip whose origin is occupied is dropped rather than overlapped, and the drop is counted (`dropped_trips`) |
| `stop_line_offset` | m | `2.0` | | code: legacy/scms_sim_ref/mock_pipeline/run.py L2467 |
| `dynamic_rerouting` | - | `true` | | code: assumption (this engine's native mobility tiers, no external source): the `Mobility` trait and its invariants I-M1, I-M2, I-M4 |
| `no_change_zone` | m | `30.0` | | standard: MUTCD 2009 §3B.04: a solid lane line where crossing it is discouraged, as on the approach to a junction. the manual does not fix the length; 30 m is this crate's choice — the 2.5 s transition at 25 mph (28 m) plus margin — and the zone is stretched to the vehicle's own speed × transition time when longer |
| `turn_lateral_accel` | m/s² | `5.5` | | code: SUMO netconvert --junctions.limit-turn-speed, default 5.5 ("limits speed on junctions to an average lateral acceleration of at most FLOAT m/s^2") |
| `junction_clearance` | - | `true` | | standard: UVC §11-202(a)1 / NY VTL §1111(a)1: a driver facing a green shall yield to vehicles lawfully within the intersection; NY VTL §1175: no driver shall enter an intersection unless there is space on the opposite side |
| `kerbside` | s, m, 1 | `{"bus_dwell_cv": 0.6, "bus_dwell_mean_s": 60.0, "bus_stop_spacing_m": 260.0, ...` | | standard: crate::kerbside: bus dwell TCRP Report 100 (TCQSM 2nd ed.) Part 4, 60 s downtown default, c_v 0.6 (secondary); stop spacing, taxi share and dwell, delivery share and dwell are choices recorded on the module |
| `driver_styles` | - | `true` | | paper: crate::style: cautious / normal / assertive below the 15th, between, and above the 85th percentile of the free-speed draw; faster drivers follow closer (Evans &amp; Wasielewski 1982, 1983; secondary); multipliers a choice that keeps the fleet means |
| `heavy_turns` | - | `true` | | standard: AASHTO Green Book 2018 §2.1.3: minimum turning paths drawn for 10 mph or less (secondary) |

**Equations.**

- *integration*: `v ← clamp(v + a·Δt, 0, v0); s ← s + v·Δt` the *new* speed carries the step, which is the legacy engine's order [run.py L2493-2495] and what keeps a decelerating vehicle from rolling through a stop line
- *published position*: `pos = point on the driven path at s − length (walked back over the lanes behind); heading = atan2(front − rear)` `s` is the front bumper and `Kinematics::pos` is the rear-axle centre; the class table gives no wheelbase, so the rear bumper stands in for the rear axle. The heading is the body's, from rear to front, so it turns continuously through a junction. The legacy parity mode keeps the reference engine's placement, clamped to the front's lane
- *stop-line braking*: `a = max(a_IDM, −v²/(2·(s − s0))) for a standing virtual obstacle` a virtual stop-line obstacle is braked for at max(a_IDM, −v²/(2·(s − s0))): the constant-acceleration heuristic (Kesting, Treiber &amp; Helbing 2010, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A 368:4585) for a standing obstacle, which stops at the line with the least deceleration that does, instead of the IDM's over-reaction to an obstacle that appears at a signal change
- *turn speed*: <code>v_turn = min(v_limit, sqrt(a_lat · L / &#124;Δψ&#124))</code> a junction connector of length L turning through Δψ, driven at an average lateral acceleration a_lat = 5.5 m/s² (SUMO netconvert --junctions.limit-turn-speed default)
- *anticipation*: `v0 ← min(v0, sqrt(v_next² + 2·b·d))` for each lane ahead on the route within the lookahead, d metres away with limit (or turn speed) v_next: the vehicle slows at its comfortable deceleration b before the boundary instead of having its speed cut at it

**Assumptions.**

- Every decision in a step is a function of the start-of-step state of every actor (the Jacobi update).
- Actor ids are assigned in demand-stream order (invariant I-M2), and every output list is ordered by actor id (I-M1).
- Between steps, consumers extrapolate at constant velocity (invariant I-M4).
- A red signal, a junction to give way at and a curve-speed cap all reach the vehicle as a virtual leader, so one equation produces every deceleration.
- The published reference point is the rear bumper, standing in for the rear-axle centre.
- Outside the legacy parity mode: a lane change is refused inside the no-change zone before a junction, while the body still overhangs the previous lane, when the target lane cannot make the route's next movement, and when another vehicle has already taken the same gap this step (actor-id order); the route is shifted onto the new lane movement by movement.
- Outside the legacy parity mode: a vehicle holds at the stop line while a vehicle already inside the junction on a crossing movement has not cleared the shared conflict zone, or while its exit has no room behind a standing queue; inside the junction it gives way at a crossing to a vehicle that reaches it first, and follows one merging ahead onto the same exit.
- A vehicle that chose to go on amber is committed to clearing the junction and does not slow for the turn ahead until it has entered.
- Vulnerable road users (VruPopulation): pedestrians are placed on a random walkable lane and walk a random chain of connected walkable lanes with the social-force model; cyclists ride between random bicycle-admitting lanes on the bicycle lane graph with the car-following model and the SUMO bicycle vType (20 km/h, 1.2 m/s², 3.0 m/s², 0.5 m, tau 1 s). Each one that finishes is replaced.
- A trip whose origin has no room waits, oldest first, up to 120 s (SUMO's insertion queue), holding the actor id it was given when it first asked.

**Limitations.**

- A lane change moves the vehicle into the target lane's frame at the *start* of the transition and slides the lateral offset to zero over it; the vehicle is therefore in the target lane for the whole transition, which is the legacy engine's behaviour and not a sublane model.
- A trip whose origin is occupied is dropped rather than queued.

**Ignores.**

- Everything the SUMO tier does that the native models do not: driver imperfection, action step length, cooperative lane changes, the junction `request` matrices, pedestrian striping.

**Sources.**

- code: assumption (this engine's native mobility tiers, no external source): the `Mobility` trait and its invariants I-M1, I-M2, I-M4

### `mobility/routing/dijkstra`

Dijkstra on the lane graph with edge cost = length / speed limit, honouring turn restrictions and lane-class masks.

version `1.0.0`; tiers `abstract`, `medium`, `high`; hosting `in-process`; draws no random numbers.

| Parameter | Unit | Default | Range | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `classes` | - | `["car"]` | | code: assumption (this engine's world format, no external source): a lane carries the class mask that may use it |
| `allow_uturn` | - | `false` | | code: edge cost = length / speed limit; closures raise the cost to infinity, from the legacy `roads.py` `CustomNetwork` |
| `max_settled` | - | `2000000` | | code: an engineering bound, not a model parameter: it stops a pathological query rather than shaping a route |

**Equations.**

- *edge cost*: `c(lane) = length_m / speed_limit_mps` free-flow travel time; a closed lane has no cost at all and is not in the graph, which is how "raise the cost to infinity" is implemented without infinities in the arithmetic

**Assumptions.**

- A node is a lane and an arc is a permitted connection, which is the only graph a turn restriction can be expressed on.
- Equal-cost paths are resolved by lane id, so the route is a pure function of the world and the costs.
- A motorised vehicle may only use a lane whose kind is for motor traffic, whatever the lane's class mask says.

**Limitations.**

- One shortest path: no route-choice heterogeneity, no stochastic assignment (ignored by every tier).

**Ignores.**

- SUMO's `duarouter` and its rerouters, which serve the high tier.

**Sources.**

- code: edge cost = length / speed limit; closures raise the cost to infinity, from the legacy `roads.py` `CustomNetwork`

### `mobility/tiered/meso-micro`

Microscopic traffic (the native engine) inside a focus region and the mesoscopic queue network everywhere else, with vehicles handed across the boundary under one id, route and driver, and spill-back crossing it both ways.

version `1.0.0`; tiers `medium`, `abstract`; hosting `in-process`; draws random numbers.

| Parameter | Unit | Default | Range | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `region` | m | `{"centre_m": [0.0, 0.0], "kind": "circle", "radius_m": 500.0}` | | code: this crate: the coupling rules of crate::meso::tiered (hand-in on admission, hand-out with holds), with the scenario's focus region as the region |
| `meso` | - | `{"jam_threshold": null, "junction_control": true, "segment_length_m": 98.0, "...` | | code: see mobility/meso/queue's card |

**Assumptions.**

- A lane is microscopic when its midpoint is in the region; a junction's internal lane when the junction is.
- A vehicle handed in enters at the start of its next lane at the smaller of its desired speed and the lane's limit, within the step it left its queue.
- A vehicle handed out keeps its position; the queue gives it a free-flow time over the rest of the segment from the end of the step.

**Limitations.**

- A hand-in is timed to the step it happens in, not to its instant within it.
- Pedestrians and cyclists stay in the microscopic tier wherever they are.

### `signals/nema-dual-ring`

The NEMA dual-ring eight-phase actuated controller (`traffic.signals.control: nema`): two rings timing concurrently and crossing each barrier together, minimum green, passage, gap-out and max-out, yellow and red clearance, protected and protected-permissive lefts with the flashing yellow arrow, pedestrian intervals on push-button calls, coordination with force-offs, and priority service; the rings are re-projected into each mapped junction's plan, and junctions that do not map keep the single-ring controller. Re-implemented from FHWA STM 2nd ed. and NEMA TS 2-2016; SUMO was read for behaviour only.

version `1.0.0`; tiers `medium`; hosting `in-process`; draws no random numbers.

**Equations.**

- *gap-out*: `a green ends when green ≥ min_green, no detection for passage_s, and a conflicting call waits` STM 2nd ed. §5.3.2
- *max-out*: `a green ends at max_green after a conflicting call` STM 2nd ed. §5.3.3, Exhibit 6-9
- *barrier*: `ring 1 and ring 2 leave a barrier group only when both have ended their clearance` STM 2nd ed. §5.1.2, Exhibit 5-3
- *yellow change*: `y = t + v / (2a + 2Gg)` STM 2nd ed. Equation 6-1 (ITE)

**Sources.**

- standard: FHWA Signal Timing Manual 2nd ed. (NCHRP Report 812, 2015): ch. 5 (§5.1.2 Exhibit 5-3 dual ring, barriers; §5.3 actuated operation), ch. 6 (Exhibits 6-3, 6-4, 6-9; Equation 6-1). each timing default cites its exhibit in `crate::nema::PhaseTiming`
- standard: MUTCD 2009 ch. 4D (signal indications, flashing yellow arrow) and 4E (pedestrian intervals, 3.5 ft/s walking speed)
- standard: NEMA TS 2-2016 (paywalled; not read: the STM is the working text). cited for the controller and conflict-monitor terms only
- code: SUMO NEMA controller documentation (parameter names and behaviour only). read for behaviour only; no code was copied

## net

### `net/gn-btp/en302636`

Exact ETSI GeoNetworking and BTP header sizes (Basic 4, Common 8, LPV 24, SPV 20, SHB 40, TSB 40, GBC/GAC 56, GUC 60, BEACON 36, BTP 4, LLC/SNAP 8) and the itsGnMaxSduSize MTU rule. Fragments nothing: oversize content is segmented at the facilities layer.

version `1.0.0`; tiers `abstract`, `medium`, `high`; hosting `in-process`; draws no random numbers.

| Parameter | Unit | Default | Range | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `its_gn_max_sdu_size` | B | `1398` | [64, 9000] | standard: ETSI EN 302 636-4-1 V1.4.1 Annex H item 8 (itsGnMaxSduSize = 1 398 octets) |
| `mtu_al_bytes` | B | `1500` | [64, 9000] | standard: ETSI EN 302 636-4-1 V1.4.1 Annex H item 8 quotes MTU_AL = 1 500 in the itsGnMaxSduSize calculation; §9.2.3 gives the rule MTU_GN &lt;= MTU_AL - GEO_MAX |
| `max_gn_header_bytes` | B | `88` | [60, 255] | standard: ETSI EN 302 636-4-1 V1.4.1 Annex H item 9 (itsGnMaxGeoNetworkingHeaderSize = 88) |
| `max_gn_security_bytes` | B | `0` | [0, 255] | standard: ETSI EN 302 636-4-1 V1.4.1 Annex H item 8 (GNSEC_MAX = 0 in the quoted calculation) |

**Equations.**

- *header size*: `H = GN(transport) + BTP + [LLC/SNAP]` GN(SHB) = 4 + 8 + 24 + 4 = 40; GN(GBC) = 4 + 8 + 2 + 2 + 24 + 4 + 4 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 56; GN(GUC) = 4 + 8 + 2 + 2 + 24 + 20 = 60; BTP-A and BTP-B are 4 each. Below a secured CAM on ITS-G5: 8 + 40 + 4 = 52.
- *MTU rule*: `MTU = min(itsGnMaxSduSize, MTU_AL - GN_MAX - GNSEC_MAX) = min(1398, 1500 - 88 - 0) = 1398` EN 302 636-4-1 §9.2.3 states MTU_GN &lt;= MTU_AL - GEO_MAX; Annex H items 8-9 give itsGnMaxSduSize = 1 398 and GN_MAX = 88, both VERIFIED. The identity '1 398 = 1 500 - 88 - 0' quoted in secondary sources does not evaluate (1 500 - 88 = 1 412), so the two verified numbers are kept separate and the smaller binds. GN_MAX is a provisioned ceiling that already includes a security allowance, which is why it exceeds the largest header this model sizes (GUC 60 + BTP 4).

**Assumptions.**

- ITS-G5 framing: the eight LLC/SNAP octets are counted at this layer when NetMeta::include_llc_snap is set, which is the default for the GeoNetworking constructors, because the documented 52-octet figure below a secured CAM includes them. Invariant I-N1 requires that the MAC model then does not count them again.
- One position vector per packet, of the size its transport type's table specifies; the optional GN extension headers (secured-packet, IPv6 adaptation) are out of scope at these tiers.
- Header sizes are exact; the header's octets are not synthesised (see the crate documentation).

**Limitations.**

- The LLC/SNAP figure of 8 octets is DERIVED from IEEE 802.2 plus SNAP (DSAP/SSAP 0xAA, control 0x03, OUI 00-00-00, EtherType). EN 302 663 §4.3.1 Figure 3 shows "IEEE/ISO/IEC 8802-2 with SNAP" but does not quote the octet count, and TS 102 636-4-2 V1.1.1 does not contain it.
- The 52-octet total below a secured CAM is DERIVED by addition from three VERIFIED sizes; no capture was measured against it.
- The identity '1 398 = 1 500 - 88 - 0' that secondary sources quote for itsGnMaxSduSize does not evaluate: 1 500 - 88 is 1 412, and 1 398 + 88 is 1 486, so the MTU_AL the MIB's own subtraction used was not 1 500. The two Annex H values (1 398 and 88) are VERIFIED and are both kept; the MTU is the smaller of the MIB value and §9.2.3's rule, and no source is stretched to make the quoted subtraction come out.
- GeoNetworking does not fragment: the full text of EN 302 636-4-1 V1.4.1 contains zero occurrences of "fragment" (VERIFIED by absence). An oversize SDU is refused here, and oversize content is segmented at the facilities layer (MAPEM layerID, CPM messageSegmentInfo) by the fragmenter/facilities-segmentation model.
- The CAM (2001), DENM (2002) and SSEM (2008) BTP ports are attributed to TS 103 248, which was not extracted, and are UNVERIFIED. A port changes no header size — a BTP header is four octets whatever the port — so the exposure is demultiplexing inside the model only.

**Ignores.**

- GN forwarding: GBC multi-hop forwarding, the DENM keep-alive forwarding algorithm, the location table, duplicate-packet detection and the contention-based forwarding timers, all of which belong to the high net tier.
- DCC_NET, the GeoNetworking CBR-sharing mechanism of TS 102 636-4-2.
- The secured-packet extension header: the security envelope's own bytes are v2xw-sec's and arrive here inside the SDU.

**Sources.**

- standard: ETSI EN 302 636-4-1 V1.4.1 (2020-01) §9.5-9.7, §9.2.3, Tables 11-17, Annex H. Header sizes and the MTU rule, all VERIFIED.
- standard: ETSI EN 302 636-5-1 V2.2.1 (2019-05) §7.2-7.3, Tables 1-3. BTP-A and BTP-B, 4 octets each, VERIFIED.
- standard: ETSI TS 103 301 CSP_PortNo tables — well-known BTP ports (MAPEM 2003, SPATEM 2004, IVIM 2006, SREM 2007, RTCMEM 2013)
- paper: ETSI EN 302 636-4-1 V1.4.1 §9.5-9.7, Tables 11-17 and Annex H, and EN 302 636-5-1 V2.2.1 §7.2-7.3 — the clauses these sizes were extracted from

### `net/wsmp/1609-3`

Exact IEEE 1609.3 WSMP v3 header sizes: the one-octet N-header, the optional three-octet channel / data-rate / transmit-power extensions, the TPID octet, the p-encoded PSID and the variable length field. Exposes the WSM payload cap and fragments nothing.

version `1.0.0`; tiers `abstract`, `medium`, `high`; hosting `in-process`; draws no random numbers.

| Parameter | Unit | Default | Range | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `max_wsm_payload_bytes` | B | `1400` | [1, 2302] | standard: IEEE 1609.3-2020 MIB default maximum WSM payload (1,400 B); 2,302 B supported; MSDU cap 2,304 B. Quoted by USDOT CTI 4501 v01.01 §4.3.3.1.3.1 and by NDSS 2024; the 1609.3 clause itself is paywalled (VERIFIED secondary). |

**Equations.**

- *header size*: `H = 1 + (k > 0) + 3*k + 1 + p(PSID) + p(len) [+ 8 if LLC/SNAP counted here]` k is the number of present N-header extensions (0..3), preceded by their one-octet count when k &gt; 0 (UPER SEQUENCE OF, 1609.3 wsm.asn); p is the IEEE 1609.3 p-encoding width in octets. A BSM with PSID 0x20 and a payload of at least 128 B gives 1+0+1+1+2 = 5.
- *p-encoding width*: `p(v) = 1 for v <= 0x7F, 2 for v <= 0x407F, 3 for v <= 0x20407F, 4 for v <= 0x1020407F` Prefix bits plus the previous range's exclusive end as an offset; the top of the four-octet range is the documented PSID maximum 0x1020407F.

**Assumptions.**

- Only the PSID-addressed WSMP transport forms are modelled. IEEE 1609.3 also offers UDP/IPv6 and TCP/IPv6, which this engine does not model.
- The TPID octet is counted once and its value is not modelled, because both PSID-only forms cost the same single octet.
- Header sizes are exact; the header's octets are not synthesised (see the crate documentation). The SDU's bytes are the codec's own.

**Limitations.**

- The width of the WSMP-T length field is DERIVED. The Wireshark WSMP dissector and the 1609.3 ASN.1 give a one-octet length in the 4-octet minimum and a two-octet length for a BSM with a payload of at least 128 B; the p-encoding boundary at 0x80 is the only rule that yields both, and the standard's clause for it is not accessible.
- The snippet "minimum 5 bytes ... rarely exceeding 20" attributed to the 1609.3 text is UNVERIFIED and is not used for anything.
- The two payload maxima and the MSDU cap are not mutually consistent. A 2,302 B "supported" WSM payload plus even a minimum 4-octet WSMP header is 2,306 B, two octets above the 2,304 B MSDU cap, so the figures come from different accounting conventions (payload versus MSDU). The model enforces max_wsm_payload_bytes and leaves the MSDU cap to the MAC model, which is where the frame is assembled.
- WSMP does not fragment, so this layer refuses an oversize SDU rather than splitting it: the 1609.3 ASN.1 has no fragmentation field in ShortMsgNpdu, ShortMsgData is annotated "maximum size is given by access technology", and the Wireshark dissector has no reassembly (VERIFIED by absence; the clause number is UNVERIFIED).

**Ignores.**

- IEEE 1609.4 channel switching: the channel-number extension is sized, never acted on.
- WSA/WSM service advertisement semantics, which belong to the generator family.

**Sources.**

### `primitive/aes-128`

Sizes, NIST security level and per-hardware-profile cost anchors for primitive/aes-128. Declares cost and size; computes no cryptography.

version `1.0.0`; tiers `abstract`, `medium`, `high`; hosting `in-process`; draws no random numbers.

**Assumptions.**

- Priced per 16-byte block call; `sig_bytes` is the block. The key schedule is not priced separately (see the rows' notes).
- hw-profile/camp-planning-2ghz: "81 MB/s encryption on a 2 GHz processor", chunk size not stated; read per block
- hw-profile/cortex-a53-pi3b: the 16-byte `openssl speed` column: one block per call, the pattern of the linkage-value and butterfly constructions; the key schedule is outside the timed loop, so a construction that rekeys per call (a linkage seed as the AES key) is under-costed by one key expansion per call
- hw-profile/cortex-a53-pi3bplus: the 16-byte `openssl speed` column: one block per call, the pattern of the linkage-value and butterfly constructions; the key schedule is outside the timed loop, so a construction that rekeys per call (a linkage seed as the AES key) is under-costed by one key expansion per call
- hw-profile/cortex-a72-pi4-openssl-1.1.1d: the 16-byte `openssl speed` column: one block per call, the pattern of the linkage-value and butterfly constructions; the key schedule is outside the timed loop, so a construction that rekeys per call (a linkage seed as the AES key) is under-costed by one key expansion per call
- hw-profile/cortex-a76-pi5-mbedtls-3.6.6: AES-128-GCM throughput stands in for raw AES blocks: GCM is one AES call per block plus GHASH, so the per-block figure is an upper bound of the AES call
- hw-profile/cortex-a76-pi5-wolfssl-5.9.1: AES-128-GCM throughput stands in for raw AES blocks: GCM is one AES call per block plus GHASH, so the per-block figure is an upper bound of the AES call
- hw-profile/cortex-m33-stm32h563-250mhz-mbedtls: AES-128-CBC: one AES call per block
- hw-profile/cortex-m33-stm32h563-250mhz-wolfssl: AES-128-CBC: one AES call per block
- hw-profile/cortex-m4-nrf52840-64mhz: the CCM call is 20 AES calls (SP 800-38C): CBC-MAC over B0, 16 blocks of the 2-byte-length-prefixed 250-byte associated data and 1 payload block, plus CTR over A0 and 1 payload block; the figure includes CCM's own bookkeeping, so the per-call cost is an upper bound
- hw-profile/i9-11950h-mbedtls: AES-128-GCM throughput stands in for raw AES blocks: GCM is one AES call per block plus GHASH, so the per-block figure is an upper bound of the AES call
- hw-profile/i9-11950h-wolfssl: AES-128-GCM throughput stands in for raw AES blocks: GCM is one AES call per block plus GHASH, so the per-block figure is an upper bound of the AES call
- hw-profile/x86-64-openssl-1.1.1f-cookbook: `openssl speed -evp aes-128-cbc` (AES-NI), 16-byte column

**Limitations.**

- Declares sizes and costs only; a `CryptoBackend` decides whether the primitive is actually executed.

### `primitive/ecqv-p256`

Sizes, NIST security level and per-hardware-profile cost anchors for primitive/ecqv-p256. Declares cost and size; computes no cryptography.

version `1.0.0`; tiers `abstract`, `medium`, `high`; hosting `in-process`; draws no random numbers.

**Assumptions.**

- `pk_bytes` 33 is the reconstruction value, a compressed point (§9.2, VERIFIED).
- `cert_bytes` 80 is the DERIVED implicit pseudonym certificate size of §9.2; cross-checks are Rostami's 250 - 180 = 70 B delta and VSC-A's 117.
- No published ECQV timing was found, so the cost is the recipe of the operations 1609.2's ECQV performs: reconstruction is one variable-base point multiplication (priced as ECDH P-256) and two SHA-256 calls; issuance one fixed-base multiplication and the same hashes. Left out: one point addition and the decompression of P_U (a field square root), measured on the host by `benches/primitives.rs` at a few per cent of the multiplication.
- This replaced the earlier proxy (the ECDSA P-256 verify figure, a double multiplication): reconstruction now costs about as much as ECDH, not as an ECDSA verification.

**Limitations.**

- Declares sizes and costs only; a `CryptoBackend` decides whether the primitive is actually executed.

**Sources.**

- standard: SEC 4 §3.4-3.5
- standard: SEC 1 §2.3.3

- Cost rows citing the Dilithium round-3 specification are for the round-3 parameter set, whose sizes differ slightly from the FIPS 204 ones above.

**Limitations.**

- Declares sizes and costs only; a `CryptoBackend` decides whether the primitive is actually executed.

## propagation

### `antenna/vehicle/tr37885-option1`

Vehicle antenna patterns from TR 37.885 Option 1: a rooftop panel omnidirectional in azimuth on cars and vans, front and rear panels on trucks and buses, and the vertical pattern of every element, relative to the element's 3 dBi maximum.

version `1.0.0`; tiers `medium`, `high`; hosting `in-process`; draws no random numbers.

| Parameter | Unit | Default | Range | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `theta_3db_deg` | deg | `90.0` | | standard: 3GPP TR 37.885 V15.3.0 (2019-06) §6.1.4, Tables 6.1.4-8 and 6.1.4-9 (Option 1, 6 GHz), via ATIS.3GPP.37.885.V1530 |
| `sla_v_db` | dB | `20.0` | | standard: 3GPP TR 37.885 V15.3.0 (2019-06) §6.1.4, Tables 6.1.4-8 and 6.1.4-9 (Option 1, 6 GHz), via ATIS.3GPP.37.885.V1530 |
| `phi_3db_deg` | deg | `120.0` | | standard: 3GPP TR 37.885 V15.3.0 (2019-06) §6.1.4, Tables 6.1.4-8 and 6.1.4-9 (Option 1, 6 GHz), via ATIS.3GPP.37.885.V1530 |
| `a_m_db` | dB | `20.0` | | standard: 3GPP TR 37.885 V15.3.0 (2019-06) §6.1.4, Tables 6.1.4-8 and 6.1.4-9 (Option 1, 6 GHz), via ATIS.3GPP.37.885.V1530 |

**Equations.**

- *vertical*: `A_E,V(θ) = −min{12·((θ − 90°)/θ3dB)², SLA_V}, θ3dB = 90°, SLA_V = 20 dB`
- *horizontal*: `rooftop: A_E,H = 0; front-rear: A_E,H(φ) = −min{12·(φ/φ3dB)², A_m} per panel at 0° and 180°, φ3dB = 120°, A_m = 20 dB, the better panel taken`
- *combined*: `A(θ, φ) = −min{−(A_E,V + A_E,H), A_m}`

**Assumptions.**

- A front-rear vehicle uses the better of its two panels toward the other end (selection); TR 37.885 leaves the TXRU mapping to the proponent.
- The class-to-type mapping: car, van and motorcycle are Type 2 (rooftop), truck and bus Type 3 (front and rear).

**Limitations.**

- No measured installed pattern: the roof's own shaping (ripple of a few dB, the 5GAA P-190033 Figure 10 patterns) is not modelled.

**Sources.**

- standard: 3GPP TR 37.885 V15.3.0 (2019-06) §6.1.4, Tables 6.1.4-8 and 6.1.4-9 (Option 1, 6 GHz), via ATIS.3GPP.37.885.V1530

## protocol

### `protocol/etsi/ts102941`

ETSI TS 102 941 ITS PKI: enrolment, standard authorization, butterfly authorization with a separate ticket download, ECTL and CA-CRL distribution, and the TS 103 759 reporting path, as flows over queued Enrolment, Authorization, Trust-List and Misbehaviour Authorities. Message structures are hand-written and every certificate in them is sized by the real COER encoder, because build decision D5 defers the ETSI PKI ASN.1 on an inner-subtyping construct.

version `0.2.0`; tiers `abstract`; hosting `in-process`; draws no random numbers.

| Parameter | Unit | Default | Range | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `ec_validity_days` | d | `1095` | | standard: EU C-ITS Certificate Policy 1.1 Table 11 |
| `at_validity_days` | d | `7` | | standard: EU C-ITS Certificate Policy 1.1 §7.2.1 |
| `at_concurrent` | - | `100` | | standard: EU C-ITS Certificate Policy 1.1 §7.2.1 (≤ 100); ETSI TR 103 415 Table A.2 gives 20 parallel in the C2C-CC profile |
| `at_preload_days` | d | `90` | | standard: EU C-ITS Certificate Policy 1.1 §7.2.1 |
| `etsi_subject_attributes_bytes` | B | `64` | | todo-calibrate: no clause fixes the container's size (calibration pending) |
| `backend_servers` | - | `4` | | todo-calibrate: no source picks a deployment size (calibration pending) |
| `link_latency_ms` | ms | `10` | | todo-calibrate: no published EA/AA topology (calibration pending) |
| `overhead_us` | us | `1000` | | todo-calibrate: no published EA/AA transaction rates (calibration pending) |
| `ctl_validity_days` | d | `90` | | standard: EU C-ITS Certificate Policy 1.1 §2.2: trust-material update cadence &lt;= 3 months, with stations obliged to update within 1 week |
| `etsi_butterfly_response_bytes` | B | `16` | | todo-calibrate: no clause this build can read fixes the currentI / requestHash / nextDlTime block of a ButterflyAuthorizationResponse (calibration pending) |
| `etsi_ctl_framing_bytes` | B | `8` | | todo-calibrate: no clause this build can read fixes the trust-list framing: nextUpdate, ctlSequence and the list container (calibration pending) |
| `etsi_report_payload_bytes` | B | `1200` | | todo-calibrate: TS 103 759 §4.2.4 requires the evidence to carry the original received messages with their AT and does not fix how many (calibration pending) |
| `butterfly_batch` | - | `20` | | todo-calibrate: TS 102 941 §6.2.3.5 gives the butterfly expansion its shape and no ticket count (calibration pending) |
| `at_download_batch` | - | `20` | | todo-calibrate: as butterfly_batch: no clause fixes a batch size (calibration pending) |
| `ctl_entries` | - | `8` | | todo-calibrate: how many certificate authorities the European Certificate Trust List holds is a deployment fact, not a clause (calibration pending) |
| `ca_crl_entries` | - | `1` | | todo-calibrate: how many certificate authorities are revoked is a deployment fact (calibration pending) |
| `report_pre_processing` | - | `true` | | standard: ETSI TS 103 759 §4: pre-processing before collection is optional, which is why this is a flag and not a stage every run emits |
| `authority_hw_profile` | - | `hw-profile/i9-11950h-wolfssl` | | datasheet: wolfSSL benchmark, Intel i9-11950H: the authorities' ECDSA cost; no EA or AA transaction rate is published |
| `station_hw_profile` | - | `hw-profile/cohda-mk6-botan` | | datasheet: Cohda MK6 with Botan: a station's cryptography runs on its on-board unit, not on a server |

**Equations.**

- *passive eviction bound*: `lag ≤ preload_horizon + ticket_validity (EUCP §7.2.1: ≤ 3 months + 1 week)`

**Assumptions.**

- There is no per-vehicle CRL: TS 102 941 §6.1.4 NOTE 4 states that revocation of authorization tickets is not possible because passive revocation is preferred. The CA-only CRL of §6.3.5 is the one active list, and it revokes authorities.
- The Misbehaviour Authority decides on the first report. Report clustering, windowed correlation and the investigation are the MaPipeline family's, and a second threshold here would give a run two answers to 'was this device reported enough'.
- Pre-processing is charged as a second pass through the authority's service queue with a zero delay: TS 103 759 §4 makes it optional and gives it no duration, so the work is charged and no latency is invented.
- A trust-list run distributes to one station, as the SCMS plug-in's CRL distribution does: the stages from `downloaded` onwards are per-node, and a run that fanned out to a fleet would no longer match its own declaration.

**Limitations.**

- Message *framing* is hand-written sums of cited field sizes, not encoder output, because the ETSI PKI ASN.1 is deferred on an inner subtyping construct at EtsiTs102941MessagesItss.asn:105:6. Every certificate inside those messages is sized by the real COER encoder, so the framing is the modelled part and it is the smaller part of every message that carries a certificate.
- The RSU delta-CTL broadcast path of Annex D.3 — single hop, no segmentation, stations re-broadcast unmodified — is not a flow here: the air interface is the node and radio crates', and `v2xw-node`'s roadside runtime carries the role. What this crate models is the CPOC-to-station path.
- The manufacturer SOC interface and the Distribution Centre are declared as roles and have no flows: TS 102 941 §6.2.2's canonical-key bootstrap happens before enrolment and the DC is a cache in front of the CPOC.
- Re-enrolment reuses the enrolment flow rather than modelling the 'outer signature with the current EC' variant of §6.2.3.2, which changes which key signs and not the shape of the exchange.

**Sources.**

- standard: ETSI TS 102 941 V2.2.1 (2022-11)
- standard: ETSI TS 102 940 V2.1.1 (2021-07)
- standard: ETSI TS 103 097 V2.1.1 (2021-10)
- standard: European Commission, Certificate Policy for Deployment and Operation of European C-ITS, Release 1.1, 2018-06

A real report is charged its own bytes |

**Equations.**

- *butterfly expansion*: `B(i,j) = A + f1(ck,(i,j))·G; Q(i,j) = P + f2(ek,(i,j))·G; b'(i,j) = a + f1(ck,(i,j)) + c`
- *linkage value*: `lv(i,j) = plv1(i,j) XOR plv2(i,j), plv_x(i,j) = AES_{ls_x(i)}(la_id_x ‖ j) truncated to 72 bits`
- *seed chain*: `ls_x(i) = H(la_id_x ‖ ls_x(i-1)) truncated to 128 bits; a CRL entry publishes ls_x(i_rev) and never ls_x(0), which is what makes revocation forward-only`
- *CRL processing cost*: `per entry per i-period: 2 SHA-256 chain steps and 2·jmax AES blocks`
- *link delay*: `t = latency + 8·bytes / bandwidth, in integer nanoseconds`

**Assumptions.**

- Root CA, the Policy Generator and the electors are offline, as in the CAMP PoC, so they place no messages on any link.
- Service times are deterministic sums of per-operation costs plus a fixed overhead: the `medium` M/M/c tier without its stochastic variant, whose log-normal parameters the design leaves todo-calibrate.
- SHA-256 and AES-128 have no cost anchor on any hardware profile, so their operations are counted and charged zero time rather than given an invented rate.

**Limitations.**

- Availability (entity outages) is a declared hook and is not modelled: the two-state Markov parameters are todo-calibrate.
- Epidemic V2V CRL exchange and RSU-relayed *provisioning* are not built. CRL *distribution* has both paths: the cellular fetch from the CRL Store and the roadside broadcast, the latter as a point-to-point link at the OFDM rate. Contention, fragmentation and the loss process on that link belong to the radio crates, so a scenario that needs them drives the broadcast through the engine's PHY rather than through this link.
- The CRL expansion cost is counted and charged zero time, because no hardware profile publishes a SHA-256 or AES-128 anchor. A device's `processed` and `enforced` stages therefore share their `downloaded` instant, and the expansion's operation counts — not its duration — are what the metric reports.
- The P2PCD and certificate-attachment policies are declared as parameters here and enforced by the envelope in `v2xw-sec`, not by this crate.

**Ignores.**

- Certificate encryption is modelled by its size and its cost, not by encrypting: the crypto-mode equivalence guarantee (I-S1) makes the two indistinguishable in the event log.

**Sources.**

- paper: Brecht et al., 'A Security Credential Management System for V2X Communications', IEEE T-ITS 2018, arXiv:1802.05323
- standard: CAMP VSC5, SCMS PoC Implementation EE Requirements and Specifications, Release 1.1, 2016-05-04
- paper: USDOT ITS-JPO, SCMS Technical Primer, FHWA-JPO-19-775, 2019
- standard: CAMP VSC5, SCMS PoC Implementation EE Requirements and Specifications Supporting SCMS Software Release 1.2.2, 2016-11-15
- standard: SCMS Manager, IEEE 1609.2.1 Profile v1.0.3, 2023-03-15
- standard: SCMS Manager, Provider Requirements v1.1, 2024-08-09
- standard: SCMS Manager, EE Certificate Rollover (Re-Enrollment) Technical Standard v1.0
- standard: SCMS Manager, Misbehavior Report and Application Specification v1.0
- standard: Every default with its status and source: docs/reference/scms-constants.md
- standard: IEEE 1609.2-2016 and 1609.2a-2017
- standard: ETSI TS 103 759 V2.1.1 (misbehaviour report payload)
- paper: Simplicio et al., ACPC, ePrint 2018/324 §2 (CRL expansion cost)

## safety-app

### `safety-app/eebl-vsca`

Emergency electronic brake light, receiving half: estimates a peer's deceleration from its claimed speeds, applies the TS 103 759 plausibility window and the forward-collision geometry, and warns when a relevant peer ahead is braking at or above 0.4 g.

version `0.1.0`; tiers `abstract`, `medium`, `high`; hosting `in-process`; draws no random numbers.

| Parameter | Unit | Default | Range | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `decel_threshold_mps2` | m/s2 | `3.92` | | standard: SAE J2945/1 BSM Part II emergency-brake event flag at 0.4 g = 3.92 m/s² [both VERIFIED] |
| `estimate_window_ms` | ms | `500` | | standard: ETSI TS 103 759 V2.2.1: the EEBL plausibility gate requires the preceding vehicle's deceleration to be positive within 500 ms before the claimed detectionTime |
| `hold_ms` | ms | `500` | | todo-calibrate: no source gives how long a brake-event warning stands after the last supporting claim (calibration pending) |

**Equations.**

- *deceleration estimate*: `a = (v(t₁) − v(t₂)) / (t₂ − t₁) over two consecutive claims, with 0 < t₂ − t₁ ≤ estimate_window_ms and both times the sender's own`

**Assumptions.**

- A receiver at this fidelity has no brake-event flag: BSM Part II is not encoded (its cadence is UNVERIFIED) and a CAM's basic vehicle container carries none, so the deceleration is differentiated from claimed speeds.
- The interval is measured between the two *claimed* generation times, so a peer with a drifting clock produces a wrong deceleration — which is the real consequence and the one a clock attack should have.

**Limitations.**

- A two-point difference of a quantised speed is noisy: a CAM's speed is reported to 0.01 m/s and a 100 ms interval turns one quantum into 0.1 m/s², so the estimate is usable at the 0.4 g threshold and not below it.
- The host-side half — broadcasting a self-generated brake event — is the generator's, not this application's.

**Sources.**

- paper: CAMP VSC-A final report, DOT HS 811 492A (application definition)
- standard: ETSI TS 103 759 V2.2.1 §4-7

### `safety-app/fcw-vsca`

Forward-collision warning over the neighbour table: warns of an impending rear-end collision with a peer ahead in the same direction, and emits the belief-side time to collision and required deceleration.

version `0.1.0`; tiers `abstract`, `medium`, `high`; hosting `in-process`; draws no random numbers.

| Parameter | Unit | Default | Range | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `ttc_warn_s` | s | `1.5` | | todo-calibrate: the FCW time-to-collision threshold is UNVERIFIED (calibration pending) |
| `ttc_imminent_s` | s | `0.75` | | todo-calibrate: no source gives the boundary between a warning and an imminent-collision alert (calibration pending) |
| `corridor_half_width_m` | m | `0.9` | | todo-calibrate: the VSC-A zone geometry is TODO: calibrate (calibration pending) |
| `heading_tolerance_rad` | rad | `0.7853981633974483` | | todo-calibrate: no source gives the heading agreement that makes a peer 'same direction' (calibration pending) |
| `range_m` | m | `150.0` | | todo-calibrate: the evaluation horizon is an implementation choice, not a published one (calibration pending) |

**Equations.**

- *time to collision*: `ttc = gap / (v_ego − v_peer·cos(Δheading)), evaluated only while closing`
- *required deceleration*: `a_req = closing² / (2·gap) — the rate the ego would need, not the rate the peer was observed to apply`
- *same-direction corridor*: <code>&#124;(p_peer − p_ego)·l̂&#124; ≤ corridor_half_width_m and &#124;Δheading&#124; ≤ heading_tolerance_rad, with l̂ the ego's lateral unit vector</code>

**Assumptions.**

- A peer's lane is unknown to a receiver, so 'same lane' is a corridor in the ego's own heading frame.
- Closing speed uses the peer's claimed speed projected onto the ego's heading; the peer's own acceleration is not in a CAM's or a BSM's mandatory content at this tier.

**Limitations.**

- Gaps are between reported reference points, so vehicle length is not accounted for and every time to collision is correspondingly optimistic — the same limitation v2xw-metrics records for the ground-truth ttc_min.
- `required_decel_mps2` is the deceleration the ego would need, not FHWA-HRT-08-051's DRAC, which is the deceleration the second vehicle was observed to apply. The two are not interchangeable and the field name says which this is.
- Every numeric trigger is uncalibrated: no FCW trigger value is verified.

**Sources.**

- paper: CAMP VSC-A final report, DOT HS 811 492A (application definition)
- paper: FHWA-HRT-08-051, Surrogate Safety Assessment Model (time to collision, 1.5 s conflict threshold)

### `safety-app/ima-vsca`

Intersection movement assist over the neighbour table: extrapolates both paths at constant velocity, warns when the ego and a crossing peer reach the conflict point together, and emits the belief-side post-encroachment time.

version `0.1.0`; tiers `abstract`, `medium`, `high`; hosting `in-process`; draws no random numbers.

| Parameter | Unit | Default | Range | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `tti_warn_s` | s | `4.0` | | todo-calibrate: the IMA time-to-intersection threshold is UNVERIFIED: it is not in the accessible VSC-A report (calibration pending) |
| `pet_warn_s` | s | `1.5` | | todo-calibrate: no source gives the post-encroachment time at which an intersection application should warn; the PET threshold itself is UNVERIFIED (calibration pending) |
| `pet_conflict_s` | s | `5.0` | | todo-calibrate: the PET threshold is UNVERIFIED (calibration pending) |
| `moving_threshold_mps` | m/s | `0.5` | | todo-calibrate: no source gives the speed below which a crossing path is undefined (calibration pending) |
| `range_m` | m | `150.0` | | todo-calibrate: the evaluation horizon is an implementation choice (calibration pending) |

**Equations.**

- *conflict point*: `solve p_ego + t·v_ego = p_peer + s·v_peer by Cramer's rule; a determinant below 1e-9 is treated as parallel`
- *post-encroachment time*: <code>pet = &#124;t_ego − t_peer&#124;, the interval between one road user leaving the conflict point and the other arriving</code>

**Assumptions.**

- Both paths are straight and both speeds constant over the prediction horizon, which is the constant-velocity extrapolation VSC-A's own IMA description assumes for a stop-sign-controlled or uncontrolled intersection.
- The intersection's geometry is not read: the conflict point is where the two reported paths cross, which needs no map and therefore works on a node that has none.

**Limitations.**

- Road users are points: neither vehicle's extent beyond the conflict point is accounted for, so the post-encroachment time is an over-estimate of the safety margin in exactly the way v2xw-metrics records for its cell-based pet.
- A curving approach is a straight line here, so a vehicle turning into the ego's path is seen late.
- Every numeric trigger is uncalibrated: no IMA trigger value is verified.

**Sources.**

- paper: CAMP VSC-A final report, DOT HS 811 492A (application definition)
- paper: FHWA-HRT-08-051, Surrogate Safety Assessment Model (post-encroachment time)

## verification-policy

### `verification-policy/on-demand`

Verify only the messages a safety application marks relevant; deliver the rest to the applications flagged as unverified.

version `0.1.0`; tiers `medium`, `high`; hosting `in-process`; draws no random numbers.

| Parameter | Unit | Default | Range | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `relevance_threshold` | ratio | `0.5` | [0.0, 1.0] | todo-calibrate: the relevance score above which a message is verified (calibration pending) |

**Limitations.**

- A message delivered unverified is delivered: an application acting on it is acting on an unauthenticated claim, and the `unverified_ratio` telemetry field is what makes that visible.

**Sources.**

- paper: Krishnan &amp; Weimerskirch, 'Verify-on-Demand', SAE Int. J. Passenger Cars - Mech. Syst. 4:536-546, 2011 [cited via ePrint 2022/133 ref. 7]

### `verification-policy/prioritized`

Order the verification queue by application relevance and by how close the sender claims to be; drop the oldest entry when the queue overflows.

version `0.1.0`; tiers `medium`, `high`; hosting `in-process`; draws no random numbers.

| Parameter | Unit | Default | Range | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `horizon_m` | m | `300.0` | [1.0, 10000.0] | todo-calibrate: distance beyond which proximity adds no priority (calibration pending) |

**Equations.**

- *priority*: `priority = round(1000 * relevance) + round(1000 * max(0, 1 - d/horizon)), where d is the distance from the node's believed position to the claimed one`

**Assumptions.**

- Distance is computed from the *claimed* position, because that is all a receiver has before verification — which means an attacker can raise its own priority by claiming to be close, and that is a real property of the policy rather than a modelling error.

**Sources.**

- todo-calibrate: assumption, no external source (prioritized policy: 'priority by relevance score and distance; oldest-drop when the queue exceeds queue_depth')

### `verification-policy/verify-all`

Verify every received SPDU in arrival order; drop on queue overflow. Nothing unverified reaches an application.

version `0.1.0`; tiers `abstract`, `medium`, `high`; hosting `in-process`; draws no random numbers.

**Assumptions.**

- An overflowing queue refuses the newcomer rather than shedding the oldest, so the messages that survive are the ones that arrived while there was room.

**Sources.**

- standard: IEEE 1609.2-2022 clause 5.2: the default receiver behaviour, against which the two relaxations below are measured

## vru

### `vru/pedestrian/social-force`

Pedestrians by the Helbing and Molnár force model: a relaxation towards the desired direction, an elliptical pairwise repulsion that looks one step ahead, a border repulsion from the kerbs of the walkable lane, and vehicles as borders with the SUMO crossing-gap threshold. Pedestrians walk the world's sidewalk and crossing lanes.

version `1.0.0`; tiers `medium`; hosting `in-process`; draws random numbers.

| Parameter | Unit | Default | Range | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `desired_speed` | m/s | `{"mean": 1.34, "std": 0.26}` | | paper: Helbing &amp; Molnár 1995, citing Henderson 1971/1974 |
| `max_speed_factor` | 1 | `1.3` | | paper: Helbing &amp; Molnár, "Social force model for pedestrian dynamics", Phys. Rev. E 51, 4282 (1995); arXiv:cond-mat/9805244 |
| `tau` | s | `0.5` | | paper: Helbing &amp; Molnár, "Social force model for pedestrian dynamics", Phys. Rev. E 51, 4282 (1995); arXiv:cond-mat/9805244 |
| `V0` | m²/s² | `2.1` | | paper: Helbing &amp; Molnár, "Social force model for pedestrian dynamics", Phys. Rev. E 51, 4282 (1995); arXiv:cond-mat/9805244 |
| `sigma` | m | `0.3` | | paper: Helbing &amp; Molnár, "Social force model for pedestrian dynamics", Phys. Rev. E 51, 4282 (1995); arXiv:cond-mat/9805244 |
| `U0` | m²/s² | `10.0` | | paper: Helbing &amp; Molnár, "Social force model for pedestrian dynamics", Phys. Rev. E 51, 4282 (1995); arXiv:cond-mat/9805244 |
| `R` | m | `0.2` | | paper: Helbing &amp; Molnár, "Social force model for pedestrian dynamics", Phys. Rev. E 51, 4282 (1995); arXiv:cond-mat/9805244 |
| `step_width` | s | `2.0` | | paper: Helbing &amp; Molnár, "Social force model for pedestrian dynamics", Phys. Rev. E 51, 4282 (1995); arXiv:cond-mat/9805244 |
| `field_of_view` | deg | `200.0` | | paper: Helbing &amp; Molnár, "Social force model for pedestrian dynamics", Phys. Rev. E 51, 4282 (1995); arXiv:cond-mat/9805244 |
| `behind_weight` | 1 | `0.5` | | paper: Helbing &amp; Molnár, "Social force model for pedestrian dynamics", Phys. Rev. E 51, 4282 (1995); arXiv:cond-mat/9805244 |
| `jmCrossingGap` | m | `10.0` | | code: SUMO `jmCrossingGap` default 10 m |
| `elliptical` | - | `true` | | paper: Helbing &amp; Molnár, "Social force model for pedestrian dynamics", Phys. Rev. E 51, 4282 (1995); arXiv:cond-mat/9805244 |
| `jaywalk_probability` | 1 | `0.0` | | code: a switch, off by default: no calibrated rate of crossing against the signal is cited, so none is assumed |
| `max_wait_s` | s | `120.0` | | code: an engineering bound, two 60 s cycles, so a pedestrian at a crosswalk that never shows walk does not wait forever; not a behavioural value |
| `kerb_margin` | m | `0.3` | | code: where a waiting pedestrian stands, back from the end of the pavement lane |
| `interaction_radius` | m | `10.0` | | code: an engineering bound: with σ = 0.3 m the repulsion beyond a few metres is numerically zero |
| `speed_law` | - | `helbing1995` | | paper: Knoblauch, Pietrucha &amp; Nitzburg, Field studies of pedestrian walking speed and start-up time, TRR 1538 (1996): means 4.95 / 4.11 ft/s, 15th percentiles 4.09 / 3.19 ft/s for pedestrians under 65 / 65 and over; σ derived assuming normality |
| `older_share` | 1 | `0.15` | | code: a choice near New York City's share of residents 65 and over (about one in six); no age count of Midtown's sidewalks was read |
| `red_crossing_share` | 1 | `0.0` | | paper: calibrated against Basch, Ethan, Zybert &amp; Basch, Pedestrian behavior at five dangerous and busy Manhattan intersections, J. Community Health 40:789 (2015): of 21,760 pedestrians, about 2,319 crossings (10.6 %) began on don't-walk |
| `startup_median_s` | s | `0.0` | | code: a choice below the HCM's 3.2 s pedestrian platoon start-up time; Knoblauch et al. 1996 measured start-up time but their values could not be read |
| `gap_margin_s` | s | `2.0` | | standard: HCM pedestrian critical headway t_c = L/S_p + t_s (two-way stop-controlled pedestrian mode); t_s, the start-up and end clearance time, is to be measured locally and is not re-verified here |
| `crowd_slowing` | - | `false` | | paper: Weidmann 1993, Transporttechnik der Fussgänger (ETH IVT Schriftenreihe 90): v = v0·(1 − exp(−1.913·(1/ρ − 1/5.4))) (secondary: the parameters as the pedestrian-flow literature quotes them); local density over a 5 m circle clipped to the walkway, a choice |
| `group_shares` | 1 | `[1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0]` | | paper: Moussaïd, Perozo, Garnier, Helbing &amp; Theraulaz, The walking behaviour of pedestrian social groups and its impact on crowd dynamics, PLoS ONE 5:e10047 (2010): more than half of pedestrians walk in groups on a workday; the per-size split is a choice matching that share |
| `midblock` | - | `{"corridor_width_m": 1.0, "diagonal_max_deg": 35.0, "driver_yield_probability...` | | code: crate::vru::midblock: the rate, the stopped-traffic factor and the driver yield probability are choices; the gap rule is the HCM critical headway, lane by lane |
| `fluctuation` | m/s² | `0.0` | | todo-calibrate: Helbing &amp; Molnár write "+ fluctuations" and give no magnitude (calibration pending) |

**Equations.**

- *acceleration*: `dv/dt = (v0·e − v)/τ + Σ f_αβ + Σ f_αB + fluctuations`
- *pedestrian repulsion*: <code>f_αβ = −∇_r V(b), V(b) = V0·exp(−b/σ), b = ½√((&#124;r&#124; + &#124;r − y&#124)² − &#124;y&#124;²), y = v_β·Δt·e_β</code> the closed-form gradient ∇_r b = ((&#124;r&#124; + &#124;r−y&#124)/(4b))·(r̂ + (r−y)ˆ) is the standard reduction and is **transcribed, not quoted**: the source read gives the parameter table and the model's form, not this expression. `elliptical = false` falls back to the isotropic b = &#124;r&#124;.
- *border repulsion*: `f_αB = (U0/R)·exp(−d/R) away from the border`
- *field of view*: <code>w = 1 if e·f ≥ &#124;f&#124;·cos(φ), else c</code> 2φ = 200°, c = 0.5

**Assumptions.**

- Pedestrians walk sidewalk and crossing lanes of the world; the lane's own width gives the two borders.
- The lateral offset is **clamped** to the walkable half-width at the end of every step. The border potential is soft, so a finite step could otherwise cross a kerb; the clamp makes "pedestrians stay on walkable lanes" an invariant rather than a tendency.
- A pedestrian about to step onto a crossing waits at the kerb unless its pedestrian signal shows walk (or it has none) and no vehicle is on the crosswalk or too close to yield (UVC §11-502(b), §11-203; the kinematic test of vru::crosswalk). One already on a crossing walks on. The wait is a desired speed that falls to zero over the last 2 m, and the kerb is a hard stop.
- Crossing against the signal: the legacy switch `jaywalk_probability` (off by default) draws once per pedestrian per crosswalk; the observed behaviour instead makes `red_crossing_share` of pedestrians violators, who start on flashing or steady don't-walk only into a gap the HCM critical headway t_c = L/S_p + t_s accepts (L the crosswalk, S_p their own speed). Either still requires no vehicle hazard.
- Mid-block crossing (crate::vru::midblock): a constant hazard per metre of eligible sidewalk walked, raised beside stopped traffic; straight or diagonal; the pedestrian waits at the kerb for a lane-by-lane (rolling) gap and walks a straight path to the far sidewalk, off every lane.
- Groups (observed behaviour): a group shares one walk, starts side by side, walks at its slowest member's pace and takes its leader's compliance; a follower crosses mid-block where its leader does.
- Every pedestrian reads the start-of-step positions of the others and of the vehicles, so the update is the same Jacobi update the vehicles use.

**Limitations.**

- No jam state (§2.5 ignores it). A group is held together only by its shared walk and pace, not by an attraction term.
- A pedestrian crossing mid-block walks a straight line at its desired speed and does not stop or run in the carriageway; the vehicles stop for it.
- The attraction term of the 1995 model (shop windows, companions) is not implemented: it is optional in the paper and has no cited parameters.

**Ignores.**

- Group behaviour, jam states and SUMO's stripe discretisation (medium relative to high).

**Sources.**

- paper: Helbing &amp; Molnár, "Social force model for pedestrian dynamics", Phys. Rev. E 51, 4282 (1995); arXiv:cond-mat/9805244

## world

### `world/source/opendrive`

Reads an ASAM OpenDRIVE file by converting it with `netconvert --opendrive-files` and importing the result, with the converter's own log copied into the provenance.

version `1.0.0`; tiers `abstract`, `medium`, `high`; hosting `in-process`; draws no random numbers.

| Parameter | Unit | Default | Range | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `pedestrian_layer` | - | `true` | | code: assumption (this engine's format decision, no external source): SUMO net.xml is the interchange format, and the table of what a SUMO import preserves and loses |
| `roads_licence` | - | `UNSTATED` | | code: SUMO project licence EPL-2.0 (exact wording unverified): the net.xml format has no separate license. The network's data licence depends on where it came from, so the importer claims none unless the caller states one. |
| `default_lane_width_m` | m | `3.2` | | todo-calibrate: sumo-net default_lane_width_m (calibration pending) |
| `default_speed_mps` | m/s | `13.89` | | todo-calibrate: sumo-net default_speed_mps (calibration pending) |
| `signal_head_height_m` | m | `5.0` | | todo-calibrate: sumo-net signal_head_height_m (calibration pending) |

**Equations.**

- *request bit order*: `bit(s, link) = s[len(s) − 1 − link]` SUMO writes a &lt;request&gt;'s response and foes strings with the highest link index first, so link 0 is the last character. Reading them left to right imports a junction's right of way exactly backwards.
- *internal chain*: <code>one connector lane per movement: the `via` lane's shape, concatenated with every internal lane the chain continues through</code>
- *junction area*: `convex hull of the file's own shape, the junction's position and every lane end that meets it`

**Assumptions.**

- A `net.xml`'s coordinates are Cartesian metres in the network's own frame, so the importer translates and never projects.
- Lane index 0 is the rightmost in the direction of travel, which is SUMO's own convention and this project's (vwp-v1 §4.3).
- A banned turn is the absence of a &lt;connection&gt;: netconvert has already applied every turn restriction by the time it writes the network.
- A &lt;request&gt;'s `response` names the links this one gives way to, and every response is also a foe. A response without a foe is reported.
- `allow` beats `disallow` when a lane states both, and a lane that states neither admits every class, which is SUMO's own default.
- SUMO is installed: the conversion is `netconvert`'s, not this crate's, and the world is only as good as that converter.

**Limitations.**

- Buildings, land use and material classes are not in the format, so a SUMO world has none; the propagation environment class is the caller's default for the whole world rather than defaulted from lane density, which §1.1 records as TODO: calibrate.
- An internal junction — the waiting position inside a large intersection — has no equivalent in this model, so a movement's chain of internal lanes is concatenated into one connector and the count is reported. A vehicle therefore cannot wait inside the junction.
- A `&lt;tlLogic&gt;` that controls links at several junctions becomes one plan per junction with the same cycle and phases. The programme's identity is lost, so a coordinated corridor's junctions are no longer visibly one controller.
- A per-connection class restriction cannot be expressed: a Connection carries no class mask, so the movement stays permitted unless it admits no class at all, and the loss is counted.
- Geometry is not cut at a requested boundary — elements are kept or dropped whole — so a bounded import's extent can exceed the request by one edge.
- `&lt;location projParameter&gt;` is not evaluated, so the metre frame stays in SUMO's projection while the geodetic anchor comes from `origBoundary`. The disagreement between that projection and this crate's local tangent plane is UNVERIFIED.
- A walking area is an area in SUMO and a polyline here, so its geometry is the area's outline traversed as a path.
- Everything netconvert itself drops is dropped here, including the pedestrian network where OpenDRIVE does not carry it as lanes and a signal's timing where the file only references it. Its log is the record of what was lost.
- The intermediate network is written to a file named for the input's SHA-256 and deleted afterwards unless the caller keeps it, so the import is reproducible but not hermetic.

**Ignores.**

- `&lt;roundabout edges&gt;`: only its `nodes` are read, to set the junction control.
- Lane `acceleration`, `changeLeft`, `changeRight`, `endOffset`, `customShape` and the `&lt;neigh&gt;` element.
- Actuated, delay-based and NEMA traffic-light programmes are carried into `World::signal_programmes` with their phases' `minDur`/`maxDur` (and NEMA's `name`, `vehext`, `yellow`, `red`) and `&lt;param&gt;`s, each counted in the report's `tl_ledger`; a delay-based programme runs as actuated (`delay-based-as-actuated`), and SUMO's induction-loop detectors are not imported: the engine's own detectors call the phases.

**Sources.**

- code: SUMO Road Networks documentation: the elements &lt;edge&gt;, &lt;lane&gt;, &lt;junction&gt;, &lt;connection&gt;, &lt;tlLogic&gt;, &lt;request&gt;
- code: assumption (this engine's format decision, no external source): SUMO net.xml is the interchange format, and the table of what a SUMO import preserves and loses
- code: netconvert import formats: plain XML, OSM, VISUM, Vissim, OpenDRIVE, MATSim, SUMO, Shapefile, RoboCup, DlrNavteq/GDF

**Equations.**

- *lane offset*: `d_k = -(W/2 - (k + 0.5) w) from the way centreline, positive to the left of travel, W the carriageway width and k the lane index from the right`
- *junction trim*: `each approach is cut back by r_j = clamp(max incident W/2 (+ 4.2 m stop-line setback at 3+ arms), 1 m, 25 m); then each edge end is pulled back by up to 7 m until every turn has R tan(theta/2) of tangent, R = 6.4 m (AASHTO P)`
- *connector*: `the corner of the two tangent lines rounded into the largest circular arc between the lane ends (AASHTO simple curve), sampled every 6 deg; parallel offset lanes take a reverse curve; motor lane vertices rounded the same way up to R = 50 m`
- *amber*: `per phase group, y = t + v / (2a + 2 G g) with t = 1 s, a = 3 m/s^2, G the approach grade, clamped to [3, 6] s (ITE 2020; MUTCD 2009 4D.26)`
- *all-red*: `per phase group, r = (W + L) / v with W the connector length, L = 6.1 m, at most 6 s (ITE 2020; MUTCD 2009 4D.26)`
- *building height*: `height tag; else building:levels x metres_per_level; else default_height_m; then, where roof:height > roof_spire_fraction x height, cut back to height - roof:height`
- *lane width*: `mean of width:lanes; else width / total lanes; else the lane_width_m option; else the class default`

**Assumptions.**

- Right-hand traffic: lane 0 is the rightmost in the direction of travel, and a left turn is the movement that crosses opposing traffic.
- A way's centreline is the centre of its carriageway, so lanes are laid out symmetrically about it.
- A node shared by two or more ways of the same family is a junction; every other node is shape.
- Signal plans are invented: the source carries presence only. Every plan is two-phase, pre-timed, uncoordinated (offset 0) and permissive for turns that cross opposing traffic.
- The ground is flat at z = 0. `layer`, `bridge` and `tunnel` are read and keep two ways from being merged, but do not separate geometry vertically: ways on different levels connect only where they share a node, which they do not.

**Limitations.**

- Dual carriageways are imported as two one-way streets, because the sausage-link merge is not implemented; a divided boulevard therefore has two centrelines and a median that is not modelled.
- A class default speed is jurisdictional, so there is NO default preset: an import is refused until the scenario names one. `sumo-german` is SUMO's free-flow design speeds and keeps a netconvert comparison reproducible, and is not an urban legal limit; `urban-us-nyc` is the NYC statutory default. The report and the provenance name the preset, count the lanes that took a default, and warn when those defaults sit far above the limits the source itself states.
- `building:part` geometry is not kept, only its HEIGHT. A part inside a `building=*` outline is folded into the outline so that one structure is one obstacle, and the outline's height becomes the taller of its own and the tallest part inside it (`HeightSource::FromParts`). The per-part volume is dropped, because the world model has no field for a sub-volume and the vwp-v1 building record has no `min_height` column to carry one: a stepped tower is therefore ONE prism as tall as its tallest part, so an obstacle model sees the setback above a podium filled in and over-estimates mass at high altitude. A part with no outline over it is kept as a building and counted.
- A polygon the tags place below ground, or that is a station or public-transport area with no building tag, is not imported at all — not as a zero-height obstacle and not as land use.
- A driving lane shorter than `min_useful_lane_m` is kept and counted rather than merged into its neighbour: merging changes the topology a turn restriction and a conflict matrix were built against, and dropping it disconnects whatever is on the other side.
- A movement whose two lane ends are within a millimetre has no connector lane and therefore no conflict-matrix row, because the matrix is indexed by connector. It is still subject to turn restrictions, and it is counted as `zero-length-connector`.
- Footways parallel to a road are imported where they are mapped, and are not snapped to the road; a city that maps sidewalks both ways will have both.
- Dog-leg junctions are imported as two junctions a few metres apart.
- A `via`-way turn restriction is counted and not applied: it spans more than one junction and has no single movement to ban.
- Two opposing left turns are recorded as conflicting with no precedence, because neither the turn ranking nor priority-to-the-right settles them.

**Ignores.**

- Terrain: no DEM is read, and every z is 0.
- Traffic signal timing, phase counts and coordination, which the source does not carry.
- Bus lanes, parking lanes, turn pockets and lane widths per lane: every lane of a way gets the same width and access.
- Public transport routes, barriers, kerbs and traffic calming.

**Sources.**

- code: osm2streets README (lane inference and the simplification list)
- code: SUMO netconvert option defaults (--junctions.join 10 m, --tls.guess-signals 25 m, --tls.cycle.time 90 s, --tls.green.time 31 s, --tls.allred.time 0 s, --tls.yellow.min-decel 3 m/s^2)
- dataset: OSM Simple 3D Buildings (height, building:levels, min_height, building:min_level)
- standard: FHWA Signal Timing Manual 2008 Ch. 5 (amber 3-6 s, all-red guidance)
- standard: AASHTO Green Book (9-12 ft lanes; 12 ft on freeways and major arterials) and NACTO Urban Street Design Guide (10-11 ft urban street lanes)
- standard: New York City citywide 25 mph default speed limit (NYC Local Law 139 of 2014, under NY Vehicle &amp; Traffic Law §1643) and the NY State statutory maximum of 55 mph (NY VTL §1180(b))
- code: SUMO default vType `passenger` length 5.0 m: a lane shorter than one vehicle cannot hold one, which is the threshold short-driving-lane is counted against
